item.title: Surface Smoothing based on Discrete Orthogonal Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Triangle meshes are a versatile way to represent 3D objects in reverse design, rapid prototyping, 3D printing and virtual simulation. Meshes obtained by 3D measurement, however, carry noise introduced during scanning and digitisation, and it has to be removed in pre-processing. The difficulty is to remove the noise while preserving geometric features such as sharp edges as much as possible.

Early smoothing methods are isotropic and cannot preserve such features: a simple, fast Laplacian smoothing, for example, also contracts the surface. Anisotropic methods do better. Many of them smooth the face normals first and then update the vertices; methods that classify features during denoising often look only at local neighbourhoods and are susceptible to noise, and sparse formulations such as L0-minimisation preserve features but lead to a non-convex, slow minimisation.

How it works

The method also smooths normals first and then moves the vertices, with two changes. A face’s normal is estimated not from a single face or its immediate neighbours but from non-local similar structures: groups of faces in a wider neighbourhood that share its orientation. These normals are then filtered by fitting them with orthogonal polynomials, whose different orders do not interfere with one another.

  1. Normal tensor of a local structure. A single noisy face normal may not be accurate enough. For each face, the faces within r rings of neighbours around it (its r-ring) vote into a normal tensor, weighted by their distance and by the angle between the normals; the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue is the representative direction of that local structure.
  2. Co-aligned local structure. Faces whose normal deviates from this direction by more than a threshold angle θth are removed, which eliminates faces with large errors from the structure. The threshold is set larger for noisier models.
  3. Non-local similar structures. The search is widened to an R-ring (R > r). Every co-aligned structure in it whose angle to the current one is within θth (40° for high noise, 20° for low noise) is added to the face’s set of non-local similar structures.
  4. Orthogonal polynomial filtering. The face normals of these structures are stacked as rows of a matrix, which is reshaped to be close to square (an n × 3 matrix has rank at most 3, so the reshape makes the low-rank fit meaningful). Discrete Legendre polynomial bases are built in the X and Y directions on [−1, 1], and the matrix is fitted with them. Where structures overlap, each face’s estimates are accumulated and divided by how often the face was used, giving its updated normal.
  5. Vertex update. Each vertex is moved according to the updated normals of the faces around it, and the mesh is updated over several iterations.

Results

Cube (noise 0.2 lₑ, lₑ being the mean edge length): MSAE 0.075 × 10⁻² (mean square angular error of face normals), against 0.135 × 10⁻² for the next-best method, UNF, together with the lowest vertex error, Ev 1.224 × 10⁻³ (Table 2).
Fandisk (noise 0.4 lₑ): lowest vertex error, Ev 5.983 × 10⁻³, against 6.976 × 10⁻³ for GNF (Table 2).
Cad (noise 0.3 lₑ): lowest normal error, MSAE 0.640 × 10⁻², against 2.529 × 10⁻² for SNF (Table 2).

The method is compared with seven others: L0-minimisation, the Bilateral, Unilateral and Guided Normal Filters (BNF, UNF, GNF), the L1-median filter, the Half-kernel Laplacian Operator (HLO) and Segmentation-Driven Feature-Preserving filtering (SNF). Synthetic test meshes are made by adding zero-mean Gaussian noise whose standard deviation σn is proportional to the mean edge length lₑ. Two errors are measured against the ground truth: Ev, a vertex-based positional error, and MSAE, the mean square angular error of the face normals. The new method has the lowest value on both measures for Cube and on one of the two for Fandisk and Cad; L0-minimisation has the lowest MSAE on Fandisk and SNF the lowest Ev on Cad. On Octaflower, SNF has the lowest Ev and MSAE (L1 ties it on Ev), and the paper’s close-up views show the method preserving local features.

On a raw scan of the Angel model, the method lags slightly behind SNF but denoises and preserves features better than the other methods. On the same scanned Bunny with noise at three levels, it performs well at 0.1 and 0.3 but has certain limitations at 0.5. The authors note that, like other methods, it has limited robustness against excessive noise and irregular triangulation; as future work they suggest partitioning the mesh and fitting the orthogonal polynomials separately on feature parts (corners and edges) and non-feature parts.

item.title: Segmentation-Driven Feature-Preserving Mesh Denoising
item.description:
The problem

Mesh denoising recovers a clean triangle mesh from one contaminated by noise, for use in tasks such as 3D modelling, computer animation and industrial design. The difficulty is to remove the noise while keeping the features that define the shape: edges, boundaries and corners.

Many denoising methods based on face normals handle features by giving small weights to anisotropic surfaces, where neighbouring faces point in clearly different directions, and large weights to isotropic surfaces, where they point the same way. Even with small weights, though, the faces on anisotropic surfaces still affect the denoising outcome. Other anisotropic methods struggle when the features are buried in severe noise, and methods built on low-rank matrices are slow. Earlier attempts to guide denoising with a segmentation either hardly preserve sharp features between regions, need the number of clusters tuned by hand, cluster an already filtered mesh, or remain unsatisfactory at high noise levels.

How it works

The method partitions the noisy mesh into regions bounded by its features and then denoises each region separately, so that a face is never filtered together with faces from another region. For meshes with high noise (σn ≥ 0.3 le, in units of the mean edge length), face orientations are so distorted, or even flipped, that direct segmentation becomes unreliable; the mesh is then first pre-filtered by a convex optimisation, segmented, and the regions are mapped back onto the original noisy mesh.

  1. Why weights are not enough. In a normal-based filter, faces across a sharp edge get small weights but still take part in the update, and they still affect the denoised result near the edge.
  2. Test every edge. For each edge shared by two faces, the cosine between their normals is compared with a global threshold Nthr (the mean cosine over all edges of the mesh), and the L2-norm of an area-based edge operator D(e), built from the four vertices of the two triangles, is compared with a user-set threshold Dthr. ‖D(e)‖2 is 0 for a flat pair of triangles and grows as the dihedral angle sharpens.
  3. Grow regions from seeds. A seed face passes its label to an edge-connected face if the normal cosine exceeds Nthr or ‖D(e)‖2 is below Dthr; newly labelled faces become seeds in turn. When growth stops, a new seed is picked at random among the unlabelled faces, until every face belongs to a region.
  4. Refine small clusters. Noise can leave small clusters behind. Clusters with fewer than 50 faces are dissolved: each of their faces takes the neighbouring label with the largest sum of normal cosines over its 2-ring neighbourhood.
  5. Denoise region by region. An existing filter, here BNF, UNF, GNF or L1, updates normals and vertices using only faces of the same region, with its own parameters unchanged. The only extra parameter is Dthr.

Results

Lowest vertex error Ev on all six synthetic test models among the compared methods, tied with plain L1 on Casting (Table 2).
Dodecahedron, σn = 0.4 le: Ev falls from 13.808 to 3.878 (×10⁻³) when the segmentation backbone is added to the existing denoiser BNF, and from 6.832 to 2.695 with GNF (Table 2).
Icosahedron, σn = 0.4 le: with BNF, MAE drops by 62.4 % (9.859° → 3.712°) and Ev by 72.0 % (Fig. 15).

The quantitative tests add zero-mean Gaussian noise, scaled to the mean edge length, to six models with known ground truth (Cube, Casting, Double torus, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron and Cad). They measure the mean angular error of the face normals (MAE, in degrees) and the vertex-based mesh-to-mesh error Ev. The comparison covers seven existing denoising methods (L0, BNF, UNF, GNF, L1, HLO and TGV; BNF, UNF and GNF are the bilateral, unilateral and guided normal filters, and L1 is the L1-median filter), and the four open-source methods BNF, UNF, GNF and L1 are also run inside the segmentation backbone with the same parameters as their original versions. Embedding the backbone lowers MAE in 23 of these 24 model–filter pairs and Ev in 22 of them. For MAE the results are competitive rather than always best: TGV has the lowest MAE on Casting and L0 on Double torus. The gains in feature preservation show most clearly on the CAD-like Cube, Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, where L0, BNF and TGV leave larger errors along the edges.

Visually, the backbone preserves features on both synthetic and scanned meshes. On synthetic models it recovers the sharp tip of the Octaflower while keeping its curved regions, and the features of Fandisk under severe noise (σn = 0.4 le). On raw scans, whose noise is not Gaussian, it keeps the feathers of the Angel and the hair and lips of Wilhelm. Among segmentation methods used to guide the same denoiser (K-means, VSA, SDF and the proposed one), the proposed segmentation gives the lowest overall Ev (Fig. 8). The backbone also makes UNF and GNF less sensitive to their parameters (Figs. 25–28), and the refinement step reduces pits and rough edges (Fig. 29). The authors note one limitation: on a mesh with extremely sparse and irregular triangulation, such as a gear model, the segmentation is reasonable but the denoised shape does not fully recover the original shape, especially at the edges (Fig. 30).

item.title: HLO: Half-kernel Laplacian Operator for surface smoothing
item.description:
The problem

Meshes captured by scanners or other sensors always carry noise, and they have to be smoothed before shape analysis, animation or rendering. The challenge is to remove the noise while preserving features and resisting shrinkage. The uniform Laplacian, which compares each vertex with the centroid of its neighbours, smooths effectively, but being isotropic it wipes out features and shrinks the surface. The paper also analyses feature points: on a sharp edge the surface is not differentiable, so the second-order derivative that the Laplacian approximates does not exist, and applying the uniform Laplacian to such a vertex with all its neighbours does not make sense. Most feature-preserving methods instead rely on face or vertex normals, and many of them consist of multiple steps and numerous parameters that are difficult to tune, especially on complex models.

How it works

HLO keeps the simplicity of the uniform Laplacian but applies it to half windows, subsets of a vertex’s neighbours, instead of the whole neighbourhood. For every vertex it generates all of these half windows, computes a Laplacian on each, and keeps the one with the least energy. The surface is then updated iteratively with these half-kernel Laplacians.

  1. The full window fails at features. The uniform Laplacian compares a vertex v₀ with the centroid v′₀ of all its neighbours. At a vertex on a sharp edge the surface is not differentiable, so this operator is not applicable there; in practice, smoothing with it wipes out features and shrinks the mesh (Fig. 2).
  2. Split the neighbourhood into half windows. Each neighbour in turn, say A, is paired with the neighbour D that is closest to the plane through v₀, A and v′₀. The line A–D divides the neighbours into a left and a right half window.
  3. Half-window Laplacians. The uniform Laplacian is computed on each half window separately, giving vectors such as d₁ and d₂.
  4. Project onto the full-window direction. A half-window Laplacian also shifts the vertex sideways, which can flip or degenerate triangles. It is therefore projected onto the direction n of the full-window Laplacian, δ = (d·n)n. According to the paper, this ensures small Laplacian magnitudes at feature vertices and large ones elsewhere, so non-features are smoothed and features preserved.
  5. Pick the least energy and iterate. A vertex with |NV| neighbours has 2|NV| candidate half windows. HLO keeps the one with the smallest energy, the length of its Laplacian plus the vertex’s distance from its original position, and uses it to update the vertex. The only parameter is the number of iterations.

Results

One parameter, the number of iterations, against three to six for the compared normal-filtering and L0 methods (Table 1).
Fastest in every runtime test, for example 1.81 s on Armadillo (43,243 vertices) against 5.68 s for the next-fastest method, UNF, with 10 vertex iterations each (Table 3).
Lowest normal error (MSAE, lower is better) in 4 of the 9 test cases, for example 9.33 × 10⁻² on Armadillo with noise σn = 0.5 lₑ against 9.59 × 10⁻² for L0 minimisation (Table 2).

HLO is compared with the uniform and cotangent Laplacians and with seven denoising methods: the bilateral mesh filter, the unilateral, bilateral and guided normal filters (UNF, BNF, GNF), L0 minimisation, cascaded normal regression (CNR) and non-local low-rank normal filtering (NLLR). Synthetic tests add zero-mean Gaussian noise whose standard deviation σn is proportional to the mean edge length lₑ; real tests use models scanned with Microsoft Kinect and the scanned Angel and Rabbit. Against the uniform Laplacian, HLO significantly alleviates shrinkage and gives much lower average vertex errors on the Julius model; the cotangent Laplacian is more geometry-aware but tends to create sharp “thorns”. Because HLO builds on the uniform Laplacian, which unfolds flipped triangles (shown in red in the figure below) during smoothing, HLO is less sensitive to high noise than most of the compared methods. For the normal error MSAE, L0 minimisation and HLO are usually the best two. The vertex error Ev (a positional error against the ground-truth mesh) does not always agree with the visual comparison, because unfolding flipped triangles can move vertices far from their ground-truth positions. HLO was the fastest method in the runtime comparison, although its code had not been optimised or parallelised.

The authors note limitations. HLO has difficulty recovering smooth sharp edges on CAD-like models with few vertices, because it is not an edge-based operator; on real scanned CAD-like models with many vertices its results are comparable to the other methods. Like previous works it keeps the open boundaries of the input fixed, which can sometimes give undesired results.
